stages.title: Deductive reasoning
stages.hook: All the lockers in the school are numbered. Locker 12 is blue. All even-numbered lockers are blue. Can you be sure about locker 12 without looking?
explain: Deductive reasoning moves from general statements (premises) to a specific conclusion that must be true if the premises are. "All mammals breathe air. Whales are mammals. So whales breathe air." If the premises are true and the form is valid, the conclusion is guaranteed.

Two key terms: an argument is valid if the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises, and sound if it is valid and the premises are actually true. A valid argument can have a false conclusion if a premise is false: "All birds can fly. Penguins are birds. So penguins can fly" is valid but unsound.

Useful forms: modus ponens (if P then Q; P; so Q) and modus tollens (if P then Q; not Q; so not P). Beware of the reverse: from "if P then Q" and "Q" you cannot conclude P. That error is called affirming the consequent.

example.q: If it is a square, it has four equal sides. Shape X does not have four equal sides. What follows?
steps: Form: if P then Q, not Q.
Modus tollens gives: not P.
So X is not a square.
example.a: Shape X is not a square.

analogies.home: If the oven is on, the light is lit. The light is off, so the oven is not on (assuming the light works).
analogies.city: If the bus is full, it does not stop. It stopped, so it was not full.
analogies.tech: If the file is saved, it appears in the list. It is not in the list, so it was not saved.

stages.mnemonic: Deduction is a lock: true premises and a valid form lock the conclusion in.
terms: A statement taken as a starting point in an argument.
The conclusion follows necessarily if the premises are true.
If P then Q; not Q; so not P.

misc.wrong: A valid argument always has a true conclusion.
misc.right: Validity is about the form. A valid argument with a false premise may have a false conclusion.

stages.limits: Deduction does not create new information beyond what the premises contain, and real-life premises are often only probably true.

trip.prompt: Find the difference between deductive and inductive reasoning on the page.

questions.q: Which describes a deductive argument?
o: The conclusion must be true if the premises are
The conclusion is only probable, never certain
It starts from a single example and then generalises
It always has premises that are false
questions.why: Deduction gives certainty from the premises.

questions.q: If P then Q. P is true. What follows?
o: Q
Not Q
Not P
Nothing
questions.why: This is modus ponens.

questions.q: If it is a cat, it has whiskers. This animal has no whiskers. What follows?
o: It is not a cat
It is a cat
It is a dog
Nothing can be said
questions.why: Modus tollens: not Q gives not P.

questions.q: If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet. What can you conclude for sure?
o: Nothing certain about rain
It must have rained, since the street is wet
It certainly did not rain at all
The street cannot really be wet then
questions.why: Affirming the consequent is a fallacy. Other causes could wet the street.

questions.q: Which argument is valid but unsound?
o: All fish can fly; a salmon is a fish; so a salmon can fly
All fish live in water; a salmon is a fish; so it lives in water
Some fish swim; so all swim
A salmon is a fish; so it is red
questions.why: The form is valid but the first premise is false.

questions.q: What makes an argument sound?
o: It is valid and has true premises
It is long and carefully written out
It uses big words and an expert tone
Its conclusion happens to be true, whatever the premises
questions.why: Both validity and true premises are needed.

questions.q: All 8 children in a team wear a number from 1 to 8, each different. Sana has the largest number that is even. What is her number?
questions.why: The even numbers are 2, 4, 6, 8, and the largest is 8.

questions.q: Match each form to its name.
pairs: If P then Q; P; so Q
If P then Q; not Q; so not P
If P then Q; Q; so P
questions.why: Two forms are valid and one is a common error.

questions.q: Put the steps in order for checking a deductive argument.
items: Check if the conclusion follows from the form
Check if the premises are true
questions.why: Check validity first and truth after.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a valid argument and a sound argument.
questions.model: A valid argument has a conclusion that follows from its premises. A sound argument is valid and also has premises that are actually true.
questions.why: Soundness adds true premises to validity.

panel.q: All members of the chess club are in Year 8. Ife is in Year 8. Is Ife in the club?
o: Not necessarily
Yes
No
Only if she likes chess
panel.why: The premises do not say that everyone in Year 8 is in the club.

panel.q: Why is "Some students like maths; some like art; so some like both" not valid?
panel.model: The two groups could be different people, so the premises do not guarantee any student likes both.
panel.why: The premises leave the overlap open.

panel.q: Why is deduction not enough to discover brand-new facts about nature?
o: The conclusion only unpacks what the premises already contain
It is nearly always wrong in practice
It needs no premises to get started
It only ever relies on personal opinions
panel.why: Observation is needed for new facts.

teach.model: Deductive reasoning goes from general statements to a conclusion that must be true if the premises are. It is valid if the conclusion follows by form. It is sound if it is valid and the premises are true. Beware of affirming the consequent.

stages.title: Inductive reasoning
stages.hook: Every swan you have ever seen is white. Does that prove all swans are white?
explain: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general conclusion. After seeing many white swans, people in Europe concluded that all swans are white. Then black swans were found in Australia. The conclusion was only probable, not certain.

Inductive conclusions can be stronger or weaker. They are stronger with more observations, with varied and fair samples, and when the pattern has a known reason. A sample of three is weak. A large random sample is stronger. A biased sample, like asking only fans of a team who the best team is, misleads.

Induction is the basis of science and of everyday learning: the Sun has risen every day, so we expect it tomorrow. But it can never give certainty, and we should state conclusions with fitting caution, such as "most" or "probably".

example.q: A farmer tests 20 randomly chosen eggs from a large crate and 19 are fine. What can she say about the crate?
steps: Sample proportion: 19 out of 20 is 95%.
It was random, so it should represent the crate.
So about 95% of the eggs are probably fine, but not exactly.
example.a: About 95% are probably fine, as an estimate and not a certainty.

analogies.farm: After a few good harvests with a seed type, a farmer trusts it, but a drought can change that.
analogies.sport: A coach sees a player score in every match and predicts she will score again.
analogies.nature: You see ants come out before rain several times and guess it is a pattern.

stages.mnemonic: Induction climbs from cases to a rule, and the rule is a probable tool.
terms: Reasoning from examples to a general conclusion.
The part of a group that we examine.
A sample that does not fairly represent the group.
A broad conclusion from specific cases.

misc.wrong: Many observations prove a general rule for sure.
misc.right: They make it more probable but never certain, as the black swan shows.

stages.limits: Philosophers such as Hume pointed out that induction cannot be justified by deduction alone, which is called the problem of induction.

trip.prompt: Look for the black swan example and the idea of strong and weak inductions.

questions.q: Which is an example of inductive reasoning?
o: Every crow I have seen is black, so crows are probably black
All crows are black, so this crow must be black
If it is a crow, then it has wings and feathers
Crows are black because I say they are
questions.why: It moves from cases to a general claim.

questions.q: Why can an inductive conclusion be wrong?
o: New cases may differ from past ones
Induction uses no data at all about the world
It always contains a hidden mistake somewhere
Its premises are always false at the start
questions.why: Unseen cases may break the pattern.

questions.q: Which sample is best for finding how much a town likes its park?
o: A random selection of residents
Only the people who happen to be at the park
Only friends of the mayor who agree with her
Only the people you personally know
questions.why: Random sampling reduces bias.

questions.q: A survey of 3 people finds all like tea. Which statement is best?
o: It is too small to say much
Everyone in the world likes tea
Nobody anywhere dislikes tea
Tea is certainly the best drink there is
questions.why: Small samples give weak support.

questions.q: Which phrase fits a good inductive conclusion?
o: Probably
Definitely always
Impossible
Proved for ever
questions.why: Induction deals in probability.

questions.q: In a random sample of 40 students, 30 walk to school. If the school has 800 students, about how many walk (estimate)?
questions.why: 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75, and 0.75 × 800 = 600. It is an estimate.

questions.q: Who is most likely to give a biased answer about the best phone?
o: A survey of only the maker's employees
A mixed random group of local people
A group chosen by a fair lottery
A large and varied panel of volunteers
questions.why: The sample is not fair.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A case that breaks the rule
questions.why: These are key ideas.

questions.q: Put the steps of induction in order.
questions.why: Observe, find a pattern, claim, test.

questions.q: Why did the discovery of black swans change the claim that all swans are white?
questions.model: One black swan is a counterexample, so it showed that the general claim "all swans are white" was false.
questions.why: A single counterexample can refute a general claim.

panel.q: A café asks 10 customers leaving a pizza shop whether they like pizza, and 9 say yes. What is the weakness?
o: The sample is small and likely biased
Pizza is simply a bad food to ask about
Ten is a large enough sample for any shop
Customers always lie when they are asked
panel.why: People leaving a pizza shop tend to like pizza.

panel.q: How can we make an inductive conclusion stronger?
panel.model: Use more cases that are varied and fairly chosen, and look for a reason that explains the pattern.
panel.why: Strength comes from quantity, variety and explanation.

panel.q: The Sun has risen every day so far. Why is "it will rise tomorrow" still an inductive claim?
o: It rests on past cases, not logical necessity
It is a deduction that must be certain
It has no evidence from past days at all
It is just an opinion without any basis
panel.why: We have strong evidence and physical reasons, but the claim is not logically guaranteed.

teach.model: Induction goes from specific cases to a general conclusion. More, varied, fairly chosen cases make it stronger. It can never be completely certain, since a new case may break the rule, as black swans showed.

points.ask: How do I make it stronger?

stages.title: Abductive reasoning
stages.hook: You wake up and the garden is covered with small holes. What is the best explanation?
explain: Abductive reasoning, also called inference to the best explanation, starts with an observation and asks what would best explain it. A doctor sees symptoms and suggests the most likely cause. A detective sees clues and suggests who did it.

It differs from the other two types. Deduction guarantees a conclusion from premises. Induction generalises from cases. Abduction picks the hypothesis that would, if true, explain the evidence best. It is uncertain, because other explanations might fit.

Good explanations fit all the evidence, are simple (do not need extra assumptions), explain more things, and can be tested. After abduction we should test the favoured explanation to see if it predicts more observations.

example.q: Wet footprints lead from the door to the kitchen on a dry day. Explanation A: someone was in the garden hose spray. Explanation B: the cat made them. Which fits?
steps: Footprints have the shape of shoes, not paws.
They match explanation A better.
Test: look for wet shoes by the door.
example.a: A person with wet shoes best explains the shoe-shaped footprints.

analogies.home: The lights went out. Is it the bulb, the fuse or the power? You test the other lights to decide.
analogies.nature: Fossil shells on a mountain suggest the land was once under the sea.
analogies.tech: A phone will not charge. You try another cable to see if the cable is at fault.

stages.mnemonic: Abduction: see the clue, then ask what story best fits it.
terms: Reasoning to the best explanation of the evidence.
A proposed explanation that can be tested.
Preferring the simpler explanation when others fit equally well.
Another explanation that could fit the same evidence.

misc.wrong: The best explanation is always true.
misc.right: It is only the most likely given what we know, and new evidence may overturn it.

stages.limits: Choosing "best" involves judgment, and people may disagree about simplicity or likelihood.

trip.prompt: Look for examples from medicine or detection on the page.

questions.q: Which type of reasoning looks for the best explanation of evidence?
o: Abductive
Deductive
Arithmetic
Memorising
questions.why: Abduction is inference to the best explanation.

questions.q: A plant wilts and the soil is dry. Which explanation is best?
o: It needs water
It is bored
It is too tall
It dislikes the pot colour
questions.why: Dry soil fits wilting from lack of water.

questions.q: What should you do after choosing a best explanation?
o: Test it with new predictions
Stop there and never check it again
Hide the evidence that does not fit
Argue louder so others accept it
questions.why: Testing can support or reject it.

questions.q: Two explanations fit the evidence equally. One needs fewer extra assumptions. Which is usually preferred?
o: The simpler one
The more complicated one
The more exciting one
The longer one
questions.why: This is parsimony (Occam's razor), a useful guide, not a proof.

questions.q: Why is abduction uncertain?
o: Other explanations might fit the same evidence
It uses no evidence of any kind
It always ends up with a false answer
It is really just a form of deduction
questions.why: The best available explanation may not be the truth.

questions.q: Which is abduction?
o: The room smells of smoke, so someone has been cooking
All cooks wear aprons, so this person wears one
Every pan I saw was hot, so every pan is hot
If food burns, then the room smells of it
questions.why: It proposes the best explanation of an observation.

questions.q: A fossil of a sea creature is found high in the mountains. What best explains it?
o: The area was once underwater
The creature climbed up the mountain itself
It fell from the sky during a storm
Someone made the fossil there for fun
questions.why: Geological uplift of former sea floor fits the evidence.

questions.q: Match each type of reasoning to what it does.
questions.why: The three types do different jobs.

questions.q: Put the steps of abductive reasoning in order.
questions.why: Observe, list, compare, then test.

questions.q: You hear the doorbell and nobody is there. Give two possible explanations and say how you would decide.
questions.model: It could be a child playing or a faulty bell. I would check for people, look at a camera or test the bell to see which fits.
questions.why: Several explanations are tested against evidence.

panel.q: A detective finds muddy shoe prints and an open window. Why should she not decide on one suspect at once?
o: Other explanations may fit the clues
Clues are always false in real cases
Windows cannot really be opened from outside
Mud is not evidence of anything at all
panel.why: Rival explanations must be ruled out.

panel.q: Compare abduction with deduction in how certain the conclusion is.
panel.model: In deduction the conclusion must be true if the premises are. In abduction the conclusion is only the most likely explanation and may be wrong.
panel.why: Abduction gives probable conclusions.

panel.q: Which feature makes one explanation better than another?
o: It fits more of the evidence and explains it with fewer assumptions
It is more surprising and dramatic to hear
It is told with great confidence by a speaker
It is older than the other explanation
panel.why: Fit and simplicity are key virtues.

teach.model: Abduction means picking the best explanation for what you observe. List possible explanations, compare how well each fits the evidence and how simple it is, and then test the best one. It is probable, not certain.

stages.title: Logical fallacies
stages.hook: An advert says, "Nine out of ten stars drink this juice, so you should too." Does that make the juice good?
explain: A logical fallacy is a mistake in reasoning that makes an argument weaker than it looks, even when it sounds convincing. Fallacies are found in advertising, politics and everyday talk. Spotting them helps us judge arguments by their quality.

Common fallacies: ad hominem (attacking the person instead of their argument); straw man (twisting someone's view into a weaker version and attacking that); appeal to popularity (it is true because many believe it); false dilemma (only two options offered when more exist); slippery slope (claiming without evidence that one step leads to disaster); post hoc (A came before B, so A caused B); appeal to authority used badly (an expert outside their field, or a vague "experts say").
Naming a fallacy does not by itself make a conclusion false. It only shows the reasons given do not support it. The conclusion might still be true for other reasons.

example.q: "Don't trust Maya's plan to recycle more. She forgot her lunch yesterday." Which fallacy?
steps: Is the argument about the plan or the person?
It attacks Maya, not her plan.
That is ad hominem.

analogies.city: "Everyone is buying this phone, so it must be good" is a popularity appeal.
analogies.sport: "Either we win or the season is a disaster" is a false dilemma.
analogies.home: "The rooster crowed, then the sun rose, so the rooster causes sunrise" is post hoc.

stages.mnemonic: Fallacy: a bridge that looks strong but has a plank missing.
terms: A flaw in reasoning that weakens an argument.
Attacking the person instead of the argument.
Distorting a view to attack the weaker version.
Presenting two options when more exist.

misc.wrong: If an argument contains a fallacy, its conclusion is false.
misc.right: The conclusion may still be true. The fallacy only means this argument does not support it.

stages.limits: Some appeals, such as to a real expert, can be reasonable; whether something is a fallacy depends on context.

trip.prompt: Pick two fallacies and find an example of each.

questions.q: "You can't trust his argument about road safety; he is a bad dancer." Which fallacy?
o: Ad hominem
False dilemma
Slippery slope
Post hoc
questions.why: It attacks the person, not the argument.

questions.q: "Either you support this law or you hate children." Which fallacy?
o: False dilemma
Straw man
Appeal to popularity
Post hoc
questions.why: It offers only two options.

questions.q: "If we allow phones in class, soon nobody will learn anything." What is missing?
o: Evidence that one step leads to the extreme
A conclusion that follows from the premises
Some premises that support the claim
Nothing is missing from this argument
questions.why: That is a slippery slope claim with no evidence.

questions.q: "I wore my lucky socks and we won, so the socks caused it." Which fallacy?
o: Post hoc
Ad hominem
Straw man
False dilemma
questions.why: After this, therefore because of this.

questions.q: Lena says schools should have more art. Tom says, "So you want to scrap maths?" What is this?
o: Straw man
Ad hominem
Valid reasoning
Appeal to popularity
questions.why: He distorted her view into an extreme version.

questions.q: "A million people believe it, so it must be true." Which fallacy?
o: Appeal to popularity
Ad hominem, attacking the speaker
False cause, mixing up what led to what
Straw man, twisting what was said
questions.why: Many believing a claim does not make it true.

questions.q: If an argument is fallacious, what can we say?
o: The conclusion is not supported by that argument
The conclusion is therefore false
The speaker is lying to us on purpose
The topic is now closed for discussion
questions.why: It may still be true on other grounds.

questions.q: Match each fallacy to a short description.
questions.why: Each has a typical pattern.

questions.q: Put the steps in order for dealing with a suspect argument.
items: Ask if the reasons support the conclusion
questions.why: Identify parts before judging.

questions.q: Why is calling something a fallacy not enough to show its conclusion is false?
questions.model: A fallacy only shows that the argument does not support the conclusion. The conclusion might still be true for other reasons.
questions.why: Bad reasoning does not prove a false conclusion.

panel.q: "Dr Ade is a brilliant physicist, so her advice on the best pizza topping must be right." Which is the issue?
o: Expertise in one field does not carry to another
Physicists never eat pizza, so she cannot judge
Pizza is not a field that anyone can study
Nothing is wrong with her advice at all
panel.why: Authority is limited to the field.

panel.q: Explain why straw man arguments are unfair.
panel.model: They distort what the other person said into a weaker or extreme version and attack that, so they do not answer the real argument.
panel.why: They attack something the person did not say.

panel.q: Which is the best response to a false dilemma?
o: Ask whether there are other options
Pick one of the two quickly
Say both are wrong without thinking
Ignore the problem
panel.why: Look for the middle or other options.

teach.model: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument weaker than it seems. Examples are ad hominem, straw man, false dilemma, slippery slope and post hoc. Spotting a fallacy does not make the conclusion false; it only shows the reasoning does not support it.

points.ask: Does it make the conclusion wrong?

stages.title: Critical thinking
stages.hook: A post says: "A new study proves chocolate makes you smarter." What questions should you ask before believing it?
explain: Critical thinking means judging claims and arguments carefully instead of accepting them at once. It is not about being negative. It is about asking good questions and following the evidence, even when the answer is unwelcome.

Useful questions: What is the claim exactly? Who says it and what do they gain? What is the evidence and how was it gathered? Are there other explanations? Is something missing? What would change my mind? Also check your own biases: we tend to believe what fits our existing views.
Critical thinkers stay open-minded and humble. They can say "I might be wrong". They do not doubt everything, since that would be impossible. They give more trust where there is better evidence.

example.q: A drink advert says "Scientists agree it boosts energy." What do you ask?
steps: Which scientists, and what did they test?
Was it independent of the maker?
Is "energy" measured or just a feeling?
example.a: Ask who, what evidence, and whether it was independent and measured.

analogies.city: A seller says "Last two left!" You ask if it is true and compare prices elsewhere.
analogies.tech: A message says "Click now to win." You stop and check the sender.
analogies.sport: A fan claims a team is unbeatable. You look at the match results.

stages.mnemonic: CLAIM, WHO, WHAT proof, WHAT else: four questions that guard the roof.
terms: Careful evaluation of claims and arguments using evidence and reason.
A tendency that tilts judgment in a certain direction.
Willing to change views when given good reasons.
Asking for evidence before accepting a claim.

misc.right: It means weighing evidence. We accept claims with good support, and doubt those without.

stages.limits: Critical thinking has limits: no one can check everything, so we sometimes must trust good sources.

trip.prompt: Find a list of skills that critical thinkers use.

questions.q: Critical thinking is mainly about...
o: Judging claims by the evidence
Rejecting every claim that anyone makes
Winning every argument that you start
Agreeing with whatever your friends say
questions.why: It is about evaluating well.

questions.q: Which question helps evaluate a claim?
o: What is the evidence for it?
Who is shouting the loudest about it?
Is it a popular claim among many people?
Does it sound nice when said aloud?
questions.why: Evidence is central.

questions.q: Why check who benefits from a claim?
o: They may have a reason to exaggerate
Rich people always lie about everything
It is simply a rule that we must follow
Benefit to someone makes a claim true
questions.why: Conflicts of interest can bias claims.

questions.q: Zara notices she only reads articles she agrees with. What should she do?
o: Read good sources with other views too
Stop reading the news altogether
Share only the ones that agree with her
Doubt every source that she meets
questions.why: Seeking other views reduces bias.

questions.q: "Critics say it is flawed" and "I may be wrong" show which quality?
o: Open-mindedness
Stubbornness, refusing to ever change
Anger toward people who disagree
Luck, since the ideas just came
questions.why: Being willing to revise is a hallmark.

questions.q: Which is an example of evidence-based belief?
o: I believe it because experiments repeated the result
I believe it because I really want it to be so
I believe it because the idea is very old
I believe it because a famous person said so
questions.why: Repeated tests give support.

questions.q: A page offers a miracle cure with no source. What is the best response?
o: Look for independent evidence
Buy it at once
Share it with friends
Believe it because it is hopeful
questions.why: Without evidence we hold back.

questions.q: Match each question to what it checks.
questions.why: Each question probes a different weakness.

questions.q: Put the steps in order for evaluating a claim.
questions.why: Clear claim, source, evidence, alternatives.

questions.q: Why is critical thinking not the same as being negative or doubting everything?
questions.model: Critical thinking weighs evidence, so it accepts claims that are well supported and doubts those that are not.
questions.why: It is balanced, not negative.

panel.q: A headline says a food "doubles your risk" of a disease. What is a smart follow-up question?
o: Doubles from what starting risk?
Which colour is the food in question?
Who wrote the headline for the paper?
Is the font of the headline large?
panel.why: Doubling a tiny risk may still be tiny.

panel.q: Why is it important to check your own biases when evaluating a claim?
panel.model: We tend to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt others, so checking our bias helps us judge fairly.
panel.why: Our biases affect how we weigh evidence.

panel.q: When is it reasonable to trust a claim without checking it yourself?
o: When it comes from a source with a good record and checks
When it is repeated often by many people
When it is printed in bold letters
When you happen to like what it says
panel.why: Good sources justify trust.

teach.model: Critical thinking means judging claims carefully using evidence and reason. Ask what the claim is, who says it, what evidence there is, and what else could explain it. Stay open-minded and watch your own biases.

points.ask: What else should I think about?

stages.title: Creative thinking
stages.hook: How many different uses can you think of for a paper clip in two minutes? What helps you think of more?
explain: Creative thinking means producing ideas that are new and useful. It is not only for artists. Engineers, farmers, cooks and scientists all use it. Creativity can be practised.

Two modes work together. Divergent thinking produces many different ideas, with no judging at first: the more ideas, the better the chance of a good one. Convergent thinking then selects and improves the best ones. Mixing them up (judging too early) kills ideas.

Techniques include brainstorming, combining unlike things, asking "what if?", changing the viewpoint, working from limits, and lateral thinking, which approaches a problem from a sideways angle. Design thinking uses cycles of understanding people, making prototypes and testing them. Creativity also needs knowledge: you need to know a field to improve it.

example.q: How could you carry water across a market when you have no bucket? Use divergent then convergent thinking.
steps: Diverge: a hat, a plastic bag, a hollow gourd, a large leaf, a bottle.
Converge: which is waterproof, available and strong?
Choose a bottle or gourd and test it.
example.a: A bottle or gourd, chosen after listing many options and testing them.

analogies.home: Turn an old jar into a pencil holder.
analogies.music: A musician combines two styles to make a new sound.
analogies.nature: Engineers copied the burrs on plants to invent hook-and-loop fasteners.

stages.mnemonic: Spread wide, then pick well: divergent, then convergent, tell.
terms: Choosing and refining the best idea.
Listing ideas freely, without judging at first.
A rough model used to test an idea.

misc.wrong: Creative people are born, not made.
misc.right: Creativity can be built through practice, knowledge and good habits.

stages.limits: Researchers disagree on how best to measure creativity, and scores on tests are only a rough guide.

trip.prompt: Look for techniques that help people have new ideas.

questions.q: What is divergent thinking?
o: Producing many different ideas
Choosing one correct answer only
Memorising facts for a test
Copying someone else's idea exactly
questions.why: It broadens the options.

questions.q: Why delay judging ideas during brainstorming?
o: Early judging stops ideas from forming
Judging ideas is rude to the thinkers
Ideas can never be judged at all
It simply makes the session go faster
questions.why: Judge later, in the convergent phase.

questions.q: After brainstorming 20 ideas, what is the next step?
o: Select and improve the best ones
Throw all of them away and begin again
Add twenty more ideas and stop there
Hide the ideas in a drawer
questions.why: This is convergent thinking.

questions.q: Which is a technique to get new ideas?
o: Combine two unrelated things
Do exactly what was done before
Stop thinking
Wait without trying
questions.why: Combining unlike things can give new ideas.

questions.q: Why do experts often make more useful creative ideas?
o: They know the field and its limits
They never fail at anything they try
They avoid all risks completely
They simply have more free time than others
questions.why: Knowledge supports creativity.

questions.q: A bridge-builder looks at a spider web for ideas. What is this called?
o: Drawing inspiration from nature
Cheating by copying other builders
Convergent thinking only, with no new ideas
Memorising a bridge design by heart
questions.why: Nature often inspires design.

questions.q: A group brainstorms 6 ideas per person. There are 5 people. How many ideas in total?
Match each term to its role.
questions.why: Creative work uses all three.

questions.q: Put the design steps in order.
questions.why: Understand, ideate, build, test.

questions.q: Explain why judging ideas too early can reduce creativity.
questions.model: If we judge ideas too early we reject unusual ones before they can grow, and people stop sharing ideas, so fewer options appear.
questions.why: Delay judgment to widen the options.

panel.q: A school must reduce litter. Which approach shows the best creative process?
o: Many ideas first, then test the best ones with students
One quick idea and no testing at all
Copy a poster from another school exactly
Wait for the teacher to solve the problem
panel.why: Diverge, then converge and test.

panel.q: Why is a limit, such as a small budget, sometimes helpful for creativity?
panel.model: Limits force people to find new ways around them and focus the search, which can lead to inventive solutions.
panel.why: Constraints can drive invention.

panel.q: Which statement best describes creativity?
o: New and useful ideas can come from practice and knowledge
It is only for artists and musicians
It cannot be learned by anyone at all
It has no use in science or maths
panel.why: Creativity is broad and trainable.

teach.model: Creative thinking produces ideas that are new and useful. First diverge: list many ideas without judging. Then converge: choose and improve the best ones. Knowledge, practice, limits and testing prototypes help.

points.ask: How do I check the idea?

stages.title: Scientific reasoning
stages.hook: Will a plant grow better with music? How could you find out fairly?
explain: Scientific reasoning is a way of testing ideas against evidence. It starts with a question, then a hypothesis: a testable explanation or prediction. A hypothesis must be falsifiable, which means some possible result could show it is wrong.

A fair test changes one thing on purpose (the independent variable), measures the result (the dependent variable) and keeps everything else the same (control variables). A control group does not get the treatment, so we can compare. Repeating the test and using more samples reduces the effect of chance.

Results either support or fail to support the hypothesis. A single result rarely "proves" anything. Scientists share methods and results so others can repeat the work. Theories are well-tested explanations, not just guesses. Science also depends on honest reporting of surprising or negative results.

example.q: Test whether plants grow taller with fertiliser. How do you design it?
steps: Independent variable: fertiliser or none.
Dependent variable: height after 4 weeks.
Control: same seeds, soil, light, water, pot size.
Use 10 plants per group and compare the average heights.
example.a: Two groups differing only in fertiliser, with many plants and the same conditions.

analogies.farm: A farmer plants two fields of the same crop but uses a new fertiliser on only one.
analogies.sport: A coach tests a new warm-up with half the team and compares injuries.
analogies.home: You test two laundry soaps on identical stains.

stages.mnemonic: Change one, measure one, keep the rest the same: fair test is the name of the game.
terms: Something that can change in an experiment.
A comparison group that does not get the treatment.
Able to be shown wrong by some possible evidence.

misc.wrong: Science proves ideas to be true.
misc.right: Science tests ideas and builds support. Conclusions can be revised with new evidence.

stages.limits: Real research is messier than a single method, and scientists debate how to design and interpret studies.

trip.prompt: Find the steps and note where repeating results matters.

questions.q: What makes a test fair?
o: Only one variable is changed
Everything is changed at the same time
Nothing at all is measured
Only one sample is ever used
questions.why: Changing one thing isolates the effect.

questions.q: Which is the dependent variable in a fertiliser test?
o: Plant height
Amount of fertiliser
Type of pot
Amount of sunlight
questions.why: It is what you measure.

questions.q: What is a hypothesis?
o: A testable explanation or prediction
A fact that is already known to be sure
An opinion with no way to test it
A conclusion reached after a test
questions.why: It must be testable.

questions.q: Why use a control group?
o: To compare with the treated group
To waste some of the plants
To make the test less fair
To change everything at once
questions.why: The control shows what happens without the change.

questions.q: Which hypothesis is falsifiable?
o: Plants given fertiliser will be taller after 4 weeks
Plants have feelings that no tool can detect
Magic helps plants grow in secret ways
Something may or may not happen to the plants
questions.why: It makes a specific, testable prediction.

questions.q: A test on 2 plants shows a small difference. What is best?
o: Repeat with more plants
Say that it is now proven
Ignore the result and move on
Stop doing any research on it
questions.why: Small samples are affected by chance.

questions.q: Group A plants have heights 10, 12, 14 and 16 cm. What is their mean height?
Match each term to its role.
questions.why: These three are key to fair tests.

questions.q: Put the scientific steps in order.
questions.why: Question, hypothesis, test, analysis.

questions.q: A student tests a new fertiliser on plants in sun and compares with plants in shade without fertiliser. What is wrong?
questions.model: More than one thing differs (fertiliser and light), so we cannot tell which caused any difference; the test is not fair.
questions.why: Only one factor should differ.

panel.q: A study finds no difference between two groups. What is a fair conclusion?
o: Not enough evidence of a difference in this test
The treatment is proven useless forever
Science has failed completely here
The data must be wrong somehow
panel.why: Absence of evidence in one study is not proof of no effect.

panel.q: Why do scientists repeat experiments and share methods?
panel.model: Repeating and sharing lets others check the result, which reduces chance and error and builds trust.
panel.why: Replication guards against mistakes.

panel.q: Why is "I believe my lucky charm works because I won" a poor test?
o: There is no comparison without the charm
Lucky charms are always bad ideas
Winning is not a good thing to measure
The test is too fair to mean anything
panel.why: A single case with no control is weak evidence.

teach.model: Scientific reasoning tests ideas with fair experiments. State a testable hypothesis, change one variable, measure the result and keep the rest the same. Use a control group and repeat the test. Results support or fail to support ideas; they rarely prove them.

points.ask: How do I trust the result?

stages.title: Information evaluation
stages.hook: You see a surprising claim online. How can you quickly find out whether it is trustworthy?
explain: Information evaluation means judging how reliable a source and its claim are. Not all information is equal. Misinformation is false information shared by mistake. Disinformation is false information spread on purpose to deceive.

Useful checks: Who made it, and what is their expertise? What is their purpose (to inform, to sell, to persuade)? What evidence do they give, and can you find it? Is it recent enough? Do other independent reliable sources agree? A technique called lateral reading means leaving the page and checking what other sources say about the source.

Be careful of headlines that stir strong feeling, edited images, and claims with no source. Check an image with a reverse image search. Primary sources (original data, documents) are close to the facts, while secondary sources (summaries) depend on someone's interpretation. No source is perfect, so combine several.

example.q: A post claims a local lake is "dry". How do you check?
steps: Who posted it and do they have a reason to exaggerate?
Search for local news or official notices.
Look for recent photos with dates, from different sources.
example.a: Check the source, find independent reports, and look for dated evidence.

analogies.city: A flyer says a shop has "the lowest prices." You compare prices at three shops.
analogies.tech: A message says your account is locked. You go to the official site, not the link in the message.
analogies.nature: A video claims a rare animal appeared. You search for reports by wildlife experts.

stages.mnemonic: SIFT: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace the claim.
terms: False information shared without intent to deceive.
Leaving a page to check what others say about it.
Original evidence such as data or a document.

misc.wrong: If it is on the internet and looks professional, it is reliable.
misc.right: Looks are easy to fake. Check the source, evidence and other independent reports.

stages.limits: Even experts and respected outlets make errors, and some topics have real expert disagreement.

trip.prompt: Find the methods fact-checkers use to check claims.

questions.q: What is the difference between misinformation and disinformation?
o: Disinformation is spread on purpose
Misinformation is always completely true
They mean exactly the same thing
Disinformation is only a type of true fact
questions.why: Intent separates them.

questions.q: What does lateral reading mean?
o: Leaving the page to see what others say about the source
Reading a page sideways on the screen
Reading the page faster than usual
Reading the very last line first
questions.why: It checks the source from outside.

questions.q: A message says "Share before it is deleted!" What is the sensible response?
o: Pause and verify first
Share it at once with all your friends
Delete the message without a thought
Argue with the person who sent it
questions.why: Pressure to act quickly is a warning sign.

questions.q: Which source is likely most reliable for the population of a country?
o: The national statistics office
A random comment under a video
An anonymous post on a forum
An advert for a travel company
questions.why: Official statistics offices collect data carefully.

questions.q: An article is unsigned, has no sources and wants you to buy something. What does this suggest?
o: Be cautious
It is surely true
It is a primary source
It is peer reviewed
questions.why: Missing sources and a selling motive raise doubts.

questions.q: Why check the date of information?
o: It may be outdated
Dates are decoration
Old is always right
New is always right
questions.why: Facts and situations change.

questions.q: A photo goes viral. How can you check if it was used before?
o: Reverse image search
Look carefully at the colours in it
Ask your pet what it thinks
Zoom in once and look again
questions.why: It shows earlier uses.

questions.q: Match each source type to an example.
pairs: A letter written at the time
questions.why: The types differ in distance from the events.

questions.q: Put the SIFT steps in order.
items: Trace the claim to the original
questions.why: Stop first, trace last.

questions.q: Explain how you would check whether a surprising news story is true.
questions.model: I would check who published it, look for other independent reliable sources reporting the same, and trace it to the original evidence.
questions.why: Multiple independent checks give confidence.

panel.q: Two sites report the same fact, but both copied the same single press release. How strong is this agreement?
o: Weaker, since they are not independent
Very strong, since two sites agree
Perfect, since they match word for word
It proves the fact beyond any doubt
panel.why: Independent confirmation matters.

panel.q: Why should you be careful about claims that make you feel very angry or excited?
panel.model: Strong emotions make us react and share without checking, and false content often uses them to spread, so pause and verify.
panel.why: Emotional content spreads fast.

panel.q: Which is the best sign a source is credible?
o: Clear authors, evidence you can check, and corrections when wrong
Bright colours and an eye-catching design
Lots of ads around the page
A very confident tone of voice
panel.why: Transparency and accountability matter.

teach.model: To judge information, ask who made it, why, what evidence they give and whether independent reliable sources agree. Leave the page to read about the source. Check dates and images. Pause when content stirs strong feelings.

stages.title: Problem decomposition
stages.hook: How would you organise a school sports day for 300 students? Where do you even start?
explain: Problem decomposition means breaking a big, complex problem into smaller parts that are easier to understand and solve. It is a core idea in computational thinking, along with pattern recognition, abstraction and algorithms.

To decompose: state the goal, split it into sub-problems, check that each part is clear and small enough, work out how the parts depend on each other (what must be done first), solve the parts, and combine the results. Parts can sometimes be done at the same time by different people.

Good decomposition keeps parts mostly independent, so changing one does not break the others. It also helps teamwork, because each person can take a part. But if you split the wrong way, the pieces may not fit together, so check the whole at the end.

example.q: Plan a birthday party for 20 children. Decompose it.
steps: Goal: a good party on Saturday.
Parts: guests and invitations, food, games, place, schedule, budget.
Order: set the date and budget first; food and games depend on numbers.
Combine: a timetable that links all the parts.
example.a: Break into guests, food, games, place and budget, then order and combine them.

analogies.home: Cleaning the house is easier room by room.
analogies.farm: Running a farm splits into planting, watering, harvest and sales.
analogies.tech: A game is built from art, sound, rules and levels, each made separately.

stages.mnemonic: Chop the mountain into stones, solve each stone, then build the road.
terms: Breaking a problem into smaller parts.
A smaller problem that is part of a bigger one.
When one task must be done before another.
A clear set of steps for solving a problem.

misc.wrong: Splitting a problem always makes it easier.
misc.right: Good splits make parts clear and fit together. A poor split can create confusion.

stages.limits: Some problems, such as those with many interacting parts, do not split cleanly, and we need to think about the whole system too.

trip.prompt: Find decomposition in the list of main ideas.

questions.q: What is decomposition?
o: Breaking a problem into smaller parts
Joining all the problems into one big one
Ignoring the parts that look hard
Memorising the whole problem by heart
questions.why: It makes problems manageable.

questions.q: Which task must come first when building a house?
o: Foundations
Painting the walls
Moving in the furniture
Fixing the roof tiles
questions.why: The later steps depend on foundations.

questions.q: You are planning a school trip. Which is a sub-problem?
o: Booking transport
Actually having the trip itself
Being happy once it is over
Going home at the end of the day
questions.why: It is a specific smaller task.

questions.q: Why check how parts depend on each other?
o: To do them in the right order
To make the task harder to do
To skip some of the tasks
To hide any problems from the group
questions.why: Order matters when tasks depend on each other.

questions.q: Four friends each take a part of a project. What is a benefit of decomposition?
o: Work can happen in parallel
There is more confusion in the group
There is less learning for everyone
There is no need for any planning
questions.why: Parts can be worked on at the same time.

questions.q: A task has 5 parts. Each part takes 3 hours for one person. If 3 people share the work equally, how many hours does each person work?
questions.why: Total: 5 × 3 = 15 hours. 15 ÷ 3 = 5 hours each.

questions.q: After solving the parts, what must you do?
o: Combine and check they fit together
Forget about the parts completely
Start the whole thing over again
Remove one part that does not fit
questions.why: The whole must work.

questions.q: Match each thinking skill to its meaning.
questions.why: These make up computational thinking.

questions.q: Put the decomposition steps in order.
questions.why: Goal, split, order, combine.

questions.q: A friend says a huge project feels impossible. How can decomposition help?
questions.model: Break the project into smaller parts, order them, and do them one at a time, so each is manageable and the whole gets done.
questions.why: Small parts reduce overwhelm.

panel.q: A team splits a poster into text, pictures and layout but never meets. What risk is there?
o: The parts may not fit together
The poster will be too perfect
Pictures disappear
Nothing
panel.why: Parts must be combined and coordinated.

panel.q: Which dependencies could exist when organising a sports day?
panel.model: The date and venue must be set before the schedule, and teams must be chosen before events and equipment can be planned.
panel.why: Some tasks depend on others.

panel.q: When is decomposition less useful on its own?
o: When parts strongly interact and need to be viewed together
When the tasks are simple and small
When you are working alone on it
It is never less useful
panel.why: Some systems need whole-system thinking too.

teach.model: Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller parts. Split it, order the parts by what depends on what, solve each, and combine them. It helps teamwork, but always check that the pieces fit together.

points.ask: What do I do to a big problem?
How do I organise the parts?
